hook.line: Tomás is answering the café's online reviews, and a good reply starts with how the review made you feel. Spanish reacts to what other people do with the same wish forms you used for hopes.
hook.es: Me alegra que a usted le guste nuestro café.
hook.en: I'm glad you like our coffee. (formal)

examples.es: Me alegra que Vale esté aquí.
Me molesta que Simón grite por la mañana.
examples.en: It bothers me that Simón yells in the morning.
It's great that you have time today! (to a friend)

examples.es: ¿Te molesta que yo abra la ventana?
examples.en: Do you mind if I open the window? (to a friend)

examples.es: A don Hernando le alegra que Tomás abra temprano.
examples.en: Don Hernando is glad that Tomás opens early.

examples.es: Nos molesta que Altamira no conteste.
examples.en: It bothers us that Altamira doesn't answer.

examples.es: Qué bueno que no llueva hoy.
examples.en: It's great that it isn't raining today.

rule:
*Me alegra* and *me molesta* work just like *me gusta*: the thing that happens does the gladdening or the bothering, and *me*, *te*, *le*, *nos*, *les* say who feels it.

When the thing is someone else's action, add *que* and use the wish form: *Me alegra que Vale esté aquí.* *Me molesta que Simón grite.*

This is the surprise. Vale really is here; it's a fact. English just says is. Spanish still uses the wish form, because you're reacting to the fact, not reporting it.

*¡Qué bueno que...!* (it's great that...) is the warm, everyday version: *¡Qué bueno que tengas tiempo!*

Same rule as with hopes: if it's your own action, there's no *que*, just the plain verb. *Me alegra estar aquí.*
smallPrint: Teachers call this the subjunctive after emotion (*subjuntivo de emoción*). You'll also hear *Me alegro de que estés bien*, which means the same.

readAndPick.es: Me alegra que tú estés aquí.
options: I'm glad to be here.
I'm glad you're here. (to a friend)
I'm glad she's here.
I'm glad to be here.
I'm glad you're here. (to a friend)

readAndPick.es: Me molesta que los clientes no saluden.
options: It bothers the customers that I don't say hello.
It bothers me to not say hello.
It bothers me that the customers don't say hello.

readAndPick.es: Nos alegra que ustedes vengan el sábado.
options: I'm glad you all are coming on Saturday.
We're glad you all are coming on Saturday.
We're glad to come on Saturday.

readAndPick.es: ¿Te molesta que yo abra la ventana?
options: Do you mind opening the window? (to a friend)
Do you mind if I open the window? (to a friend)

readAndPick.es: A Vale le molesta que Simón coma su pan.
options: It bothers Vale that Simón eats her bread.
It bothers Simón that Vale eats his bread.
It bothers me that Simón eats Vale's bread.

readAndPick.es: Qué bueno que ustedes puedan venir.
options: It's great that you can come. (to a friend)
It's great that I can come.
It's great that you all can come.

readAndPick.es: Le alegra que Tomás abra temprano.
options: I'm glad Tomás opens early.
Tomás is glad to open early.
She's glad Tomás opens early.

readAndPick.es: Me alegra que usted esté aquí.
options: I'm glad you're here. (formal)
I'm glad you all are here.
You're glad I'm here. (formal)

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *estás* or *estés* and type the whole sentence, to a friend: *Me alegra que tú ___ aquí.*
yourTurn.answer: Me alegra que tú estés aquí.
yourTurn.why: You're reacting to a fact, and a reaction takes the wish form: *estés*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *tienes* or *tengas* and type the whole sentence, to a friend: *¡Qué bueno que ___ tiempo hoy!*
accept: Qué bueno que tengas tiempo hoy.
yourTurn.why: *Qué bueno que* is a reaction too, so *tengas*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: It bothers me that Simón yells in the morning.
yourTurn.answer: Me molesta que Simón grite por la mañana.
accept: Me molesta que Simón grite en la mañana.
yourTurn.why: *Me molesta* works like *me gusta*, and *grita* becomes the wish form *grite*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm glad to be here.
yourTurn.why: You're the one who's here, so no *que*: just *estar*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, to a customer (formal): I'm glad you're here.
yourTurn.answer: Me alegra que usted esté aquí.
yourTurn.why: For *usted*, the wish form of *estar* is *esté*, with the accent.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about us: *Me molesta que Altamira no conteste.*
yourTurn.answer: Nos molesta que Altamira no conteste.
yourTurn.why: Only the feeler changes: *me* becomes *nos*, and *molesta* stays.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about don Hernando: *Me alegra que Tomás abra temprano.*
yourTurn.answer: A don Hernando le alegra que Tomás abra temprano.
yourTurn.why: Just like *a don Hernando le gusta*: *me* becomes *le*, with *a don Hernando* in front.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it to you all instead: *Qué bueno que puedas venir.*
yourTurn.answer: Qué bueno que ustedes puedan venir.

pitfalls.wrong: Me alegra que tú estás aquí.
pitfalls.right: Me alegra que tú estés aquí.
pitfalls.why: Almost. Even when it's a fact, a reaction takes the wish form: *estés*.

pitfalls.wrong: Estoy alegre que Vale esté aquí.
pitfalls.right: Me alegra que Vale esté aquí.
pitfalls.why: Spanish turns it around like *me gusta*: the news gladdens you, so *me alegra*.

pitfalls.wrong: Me alegra que yo esté aquí.
pitfalls.why: When it's your own action, drop *que* and use the plain verb.
*Yo molesto* means I bother someone; for what bothers you, say *me molesta*.

personal: Write two true reactions about your week, naming who does it: one with *Me alegra que* and one with *Me molesta que* (*Me alegra que mi hermana...*, *Me molesta que mi vecino...*).
